title: Shell scripting 101
summary: The oven controller needs small helper scripts, and its robot tester is merciless. Write bash scripts with arguments, if, loops, read and exit codes, and pass the tests.

nodes.richtea: the oven controller; your scripts go in /root

tasks.title: Hello, oven
tasks.text: Write `/root/greet.sh`. Run with a name, it prints `Hello, <name>!`. Run with no argument at all, it prints `Hello, stranger!`. The robot will also try a name with a space in it (`./greet.sh 'Mary Jane'` must print `Hello, Mary Jane!`).

checks.fail_msg: /root/greet.sh is missing, not executable (chmod +x), or has no #! line at the top.
./greet.sh {{NAME}} should print exactly: Hello, {{NAME}}!
./greet.sh 'Mary Jane' should print exactly: Hello, Mary Jane! (check your quotes)
./greet.sh with no argument should print exactly: Hello, stranger!

hints: A script is a text file starting with `#!/bin/bash`, made executable with `chmod +x`. Run it as `./greet.sh` (or `/root/greet.sh`). Write it with `nano /root/greet.sh`.
`$1` is the first argument. Quote it, `"$1"`, so a name with a space stays one thing.
`${1:-stranger}` means "$1, or `stranger` if $1 is empty". So: `name="${1:-stranger}"` then `echo "Hello, $name!"`.

tasks.title: Is the oven ready?
tasks.text:
Write `/root/oven-temp.sh TEMP`. It decides, and tells the controller through its **exit code**:

| temperature | prints | exit code |
|---|---|---|
| below 180 | `too cold` | 1 |
| 180 to 220 | `perfect` | 0 |
| above 220 | `burning!` | 2 |

checks.fail_msg: /root/oven-temp.sh is missing, not executable (chmod +x), or has no #! line at the top.

checks.cmd: t=150; if [ $t -lt 180 ]; then e='too cold'; x=1; elif [ $t -gt 220 ]; then e='burning!'; x=2; else e=perfect; x=0; fi; o=$(/root/oven-temp.sh $t); c=$?; [ "$o" = "$e" ] && [ $c -eq $x ] && t=179; if [ $t -lt 180 ]; then e='too cold'; x=1; elif [ $t -gt 220 ]; then e='burning!'; x=2; else e=perfect; x=0; fi; o=$(/root/oven-temp.sh $t); c=$?; [ "$o" = "$e" ] && [ $c -eq $x ]
checks.fail_msg: Below 180 should print `too cold` and exit 1 (try ./oven-temp.sh 150; echo $?).

checks.cmd: t=180; if [ $t -lt 180 ]; then e='too cold'; x=1; elif [ $t -gt 220 ]; then e='burning!'; x=2; else e=perfect; x=0; fi; o=$(/root/oven-temp.sh $t); c=$?; [ "$o" = "$e" ] && [ $c -eq $x ] && t=200; if [ $t -lt 180 ]; then e='too cold'; x=1; elif [ $t -gt 220 ]; then e='burning!'; x=2; else e=perfect; x=0; fi; o=$(/root/oven-temp.sh $t); c=$?; [ "$o" = "$e" ] && [ $c -eq $x ] && t=220; if [ $t -lt 180 ]; then e='too cold'; x=1; elif [ $t -gt 220 ]; then e='burning!'; x=2; else e=perfect; x=0; fi; o=$(/root/oven-temp.sh $t); c=$?; [ "$o" = "$e" ] && [ $c -eq $x ]
checks.fail_msg: 180 to 220 (inclusive) should print `perfect` and exit 0.

checks.cmd: t=221; if [ $t -lt 180 ]; then e='too cold'; x=1; elif [ $t -gt 220 ]; then e='burning!'; x=2; else e=perfect; x=0; fi; o=$(/root/oven-temp.sh $t); c=$?; [ "$o" = "$e" ] && [ $c -eq $x ] && t=300; if [ $t -lt 180 ]; then e='too cold'; x=1; elif [ $t -gt 220 ]; then e='burning!'; x=2; else e=perfect; x=0; fi; o=$(/root/oven-temp.sh $t); c=$?; [ "$o" = "$e" ] && [ $c -eq $x ]
checks.fail_msg: Above 220 should print `burning!` and exit 2.

checks.cmd: t={{T}}; if [ $t -lt 180 ]; then e='too cold'; x=1; elif [ $t -gt 220 ]; then e='burning!'; x=2; else e=perfect; x=0; fi; o=$(/root/oven-temp.sh $t); c=$?; [ "$o" = "$e" ] && [ $c -eq $x ]
checks.fail_msg: The robot tried {{T}} and did not get the right answer.

hints: Compare numbers with `[ "$1" -lt 180 ]` (less than); also `-gt` greater, `-le`, `-ge`, `-eq`, `-ne`. Inside `[ ]` the spaces matter!
`if ...; then ...; elif ...; then ...; else ...; fi`. `exit 2` ends the script with exit code 2. Without an exit, the code is that of the last command (0 for a successful echo).
Test it yourself: `./oven-temp.sh 221; echo $?`. `$?` holds the previous command's exit code.

steps.cmd:
cat > /root/oven-temp.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
temp=$1
if [ "$temp" -lt 180 ]; then
  echo "too cold"
  exit 1
elif [ "$temp" -gt 220 ]; then
  echo "burning!"
  exit 2
else
  echo "perfect"
fi
EOF
chmod +x /root/oven-temp.sh

tasks.title: Count the dough
tasks.text: Write `/root/total.sh`. It reads lines like `chocolate 12` from **standard input** (an item and a quantity) and prints the total quantity. So `printf 'choc 3\noat 4\n' | ./total.sh` prints `7`, and no input at all prints `0`.

checks.fail_msg: /root/total.sh is missing, not executable (chmod +x), or has no #! line at the top.
printf 'choc 3\noat 4\n' | ./total.sh should print 7.
The robot fed in jam {{A}}, custard {{B}}, ginger 1 and did not get the total.
With no input, total.sh should print 0.

hints: `while read -r item qty; do ... done` reads stdin one line at a time, splitting each line into the variables `item` and `qty`.
Arithmetic is `$(( ))`: `total=$((total + qty))`. Start with `total=0` before the loop and `echo "$total"` after it.

steps.cmd:
cat > /root/total.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
total=0
while read -r item qty; do
  total=$((total + qty))
done
echo "$total"
EOF
chmod +x /root/total.sh

tasks.title: Batch inspector
tasks.text:
Write `/root/batches.sh DIR`. For every file ending in `.batch` in `DIR`, in alphabetical order, it prints the file name and its number of lines, then a total:

```
choc.batch 2
oat raisin.batch 1
vanilla.batch 3
total 6
```

Other files are ignored. Yes, the robot **will** use a file name with a space in it.

checks.fail_msg: /root/batches.sh is missing, not executable (chmod +x), or has no #! line at the top.

checks.cmd:
d=$(mktemp -d); printf 'a
b
' > "$d/choc.batch"; printf 'x
' > "$d/oat raisin.batch"; printf '1
2
3
' > "$d/vanilla.batch"; echo hi > "$d/notes.txt"; out=$(/root/batches.sh "$d"); rm -rf "$d"; [ "$out" = "$(printf 'choc.batch 2
oat raisin.batch 1
vanilla.batch 3
total 6')" ]
checks.fail_msg: For the example folder the output was not exactly the example above. Make your own test folder and compare.

checks.cmd: d=$(mktemp -d); for i in $(seq 1 {{A}}); do echo $i; done > "$d/big.batch"; out=$(/root/batches.sh "$d"); rm -rf "$d"; [ "$out" = "$(printf 'big.batch {{A}}\ntotal {{A}}')" ]
checks.fail_msg: With one file of {{A}} lines the output should be `big.batch {{A}}` then `total {{A}}`.

hints: `for f in "$1"/*.batch; do ... done` loops over matching files, already in alphabetical order. Quote `"$f"` everywhere so the space in a name doesn't split it in two.
`wc -l < "$f"` prints just the number (with `wc -l "$f"` you also get the name). `basename "$f"` drops the folder part.
Keep a running total like in the previous task, and `echo "total $total"` after the loop.

steps.cmd:
cat > /root/batches.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
dir=$1
total=0
for f in "$dir"/*.batch; do
  [ -e "$f" ] || continue
  n=$(wc -l < "$f")
  echo "$(basename "$f") $n"
  total=$((total + n))
done
echo "total $total"
EOF
chmod +x /root/batches.sh

tasks.title: A script that says no
tasks.text:
Write `/root/backup.sh SOURCE_DIR DEST_DIR`, which archives a folder into `DEST_DIR/<name of source>.tar.gz` (for example `/tmp/recipes.tar.gz` for source `/srv/recipes`). Good scripts refuse bad input **loudly**:

- fewer than 2 arguments: print a usage message to **stderr**, exit code **64**
- source isn't a directory: print an error to **stderr**, exit code **1**
- otherwise: create the archive, print its path, exit code **0**

checks.fail_msg: /root/backup.sh is missing, not executable (chmod +x), or has no #! line at the top.
With no (or one) argument: nothing on stdout, a message on stderr, exit code 64.
With a source that isn't a directory: an error on stderr, nothing on stdout, exit code 1.

checks.cmd: s=$(mktemp -d)/recipes; mkdir -p $s; echo '{{A}} spoons of jam' > $s/jam.txt; d=$(mktemp -d); /root/backup.sh $s $d >/dev/null && tar -xzOf $d/recipes.tar.gz ./jam.txt 2>/dev/null | grep -q '{{A}} spoons' || tar -xzOf $d/recipes.tar.gz recipes/jam.txt 2>/dev/null | grep -q '{{A}} spoons'
checks.fail_msg: A good backup should create DEST/<source name>.tar.gz containing the source's files (e.g. jam.txt), and exit 0.

hints: `$#` is the number of arguments: `if [ $# -lt 2 ]; then echo "usage: ..." >&2; exit 64; fi`. `>&2` sends the echo to stderr.
`[ -d "$1" ]` is true when $1 is a directory; `[ ! -d "$1" ]` when it isn't.
`tar -czf "$2/$(basename "$1").tar.gz" -C "$1" .` makes the archive (`c` create, `z` gzip, `f` file name; `-C` changes into the folder first). Look inside with `tar -tzf file.tar.gz`.

steps.cmd:
cat > /root/backup.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
if [ $# -lt 2 ]; then
  echo "usage: backup.sh SOURCE_DIR DEST_DIR" >&2
  exit 64
fi
src=$1
dest=$2
if [ ! -d "$src" ]; then
  echo "backup.sh: $src is not a directory" >&2
  exit 1
fi
archive="$dest/$(basename "$src").tar.gz"
tar -czf "$archive" -C "$src" .
echo "$archive"
EOF
chmod +x /root/backup.sh
